source_text: As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts have an increasingly dismal assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher . “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” Trump’s approval rating was already low, but his latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even analysts are delivering a deeply negative assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval was already weak, but this latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either of his terms. It comes as he faces a series of crises tied largely to decisions made by his own administration—an unmistakable reminder that leaders must be judged by results, not promises.

The economy is the first major failure. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked it as their top concern, making it the most influential issue since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19, and although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump believing his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden.

Those hopes have not been realized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. But Trump has not delivered that reassurance through meaningful results, instead making widely criticized remarks such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy deteriorated under the burden of his tariffs.

The approach is also hitting Americans at the gas pump. Gas prices are approaching record highs, underscoring the strain on the Trump economy and connecting directly to the second major source of public anger: his war on Iran.

Only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Just 26 percent agree with his claim that the war will make the United States safer, and only 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices rising to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are rejecting the cost of this military “excursion,” particularly as it raises the price of filling the family car.

Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not persuaded.

source_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even political analysts are describing his second administration in deeply negative terms. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval was already weak, but this latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely created by decisions made by his own administration—an unmistakable reminder that leaders should be judged by the material results their policies produce, not by promises made to voters.

The economy is the clearest example of that failure. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked it as their top concern, making it the most influential issue since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19, and although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump believing his economic program would deliver more than Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden.

Those hopes have not been fulfilled. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. But Trump has offered no meaningful relief or reassurance through results. Instead, as tariffs worsened economic pressures, he drew widespread criticism for remarks such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30,” dismissing the hardship facing families.

That policy approach is also imposing greater costs on people at the gas pump. Gas prices are approaching record highs, underscoring the strain on the Trump economy and intensifying the second major source of public anger: his war on Iran.

Only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Just 26 percent agree with his claim that the war will make the United States safer, and only 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices rising to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are rejecting the human and financial cost of this military “excursion,” especially as it raises the price of filling the family car.

Trump may dismiss concerns about affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not persuaded.

source_text: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big screen isn’t gone yet Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years. The closure adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue, as the movie-going scene continues to change with streaming platforms and shifting audience habits. source_text:
Another cinema in Singapore is closing, but the country’s big-screen tradition is not over. Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, after more than 30 years in operation. It is now one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years.

The closure reflects broader changes in how people access films, including changing habits and the rise of streaming platforms. These shifts, along with commercial pressures, are reshaping spaces that have long been part of Singapore’s cultural life. Other theatres that have disappeared include Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue.

At the same time, the cinema experience continues to have a place. New operators such as Filmhouse, which took over The Projector, and around 30 cinema locations across the island indicate that Singaporeans still value watching films together on the big screen—even as that experience evolves from the way it once was.

source_text: Softcare's revenue rose by 25% last year, while its profit increased 27%, as its focus on emerging markets yielded solid results image credit: Bamboo Works Key Takeaways: Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, led by a 134% rise in Latin America and double-digit growth in its core African markets The strong results put the diaper maker at the front of the pack of a new wave of Chinese companies chasing African consumers The company known as the "African diaper king" has defied skeptics who said it couldn't sustain its dominant position in its core Africa market, as well as other emerging markets it has entered more recently. Many of the new believers in Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) cheered the release of the company's inaugural annual results late last week by bidding up its shares nearly 15% in the two trading days after the announcement. The company's revenue rose by 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while its net profit was up 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025, another positive indicator. Sales to its core markets in Africa rose by a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also moving out of Africa to find success in other emerging markets. The best example is Latin America, whose sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after it entered Peru in 2020, and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where its sales, though quite small, more than doubled last year to $272,000. After several years of declines, average selling prices (ASP) for Softcare's two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper ASPs increased by 4.4% year-over-year, as that segment accounted for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product ASPs grew by 7% and made up 17.5% of revenue. The ASP increases are important because they show the company is finding ways to convince consumers to pay more for its products in these famously price-sensitive markets, helping to maintain and even boost its margins. rewritten_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose 25% last year and profit increased 27%, showing that disciplined attention to emerging markets can deliver results.

The company reported 25% revenue growth, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets. Those results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies seeking to serve African consumers.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has answered skeptics who doubted it could maintain its leading position in Africa and expand successfully into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively to the company’s first annual results following its IPO, bidding up its shares nearly 15% over the two trading days after the announcement.

Revenue increased 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while net profit rose 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets grew a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also extending its reach beyond Africa. Latin America provides the clearest example: sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales there remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines increased between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices rose 4.4% year-over-year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products increased 7%, representing 17.5% of revenue.

These higher prices are significant because they show Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for its products even in markets known for strict price sensitivity. That has helped the company preserve and strengthen its margins through sound commercial execution.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

source_text:
Softcare’s revenue rose 25% last year and profit increased 27%, showing that disciplined attention to emerging markets can deliver results.

The company reported 25% revenue growth, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its core African markets. Those results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies seeking to serve African consumers.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has answered skeptics who doubted it could maintain its leading position in Africa and expand successfully into other emerging markets. Investors responded positively to the company’s first annual results following its IPO, bidding up its shares nearly 15% over the two trading days after the announcement.

Revenue increased 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while net profit rose 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets grew a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also extending its reach beyond Africa. Latin America provides the clearest example: sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024.

The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales there remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines increased between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices rose 4.4% year-over-year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products increased 7%, representing 17.5% of revenue.

These higher prices are significant because they show Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for its products even in markets known for strict price sensitivity. That has helped the company preserve and strengthen its margins through sound commercial execution.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. This all-stock transaction, valued at approximately USD 2.5 billion, will see Udemy become a wholly-owned subsidiary of Coursera. Existing Coursera shareholders will hold about 59% of the combined entity, with Udemy stockholders owning 41%.

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.

Officials made clear that IGL must treat this work as a priority and complete it promptly with adequate manpower. Areas excavated for pipeline installation must also be securely backfilled to protect the public and prevent avoidable hazards. The initiative reflects the government’s effort to expand access to cleaner energy while insisting on efficient execution and responsibility for maintaining public order and safety.

source_text:
The Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has taken steps to reduce administrative delays and expand access to cleaner fuel in the capital. With immediate effect, permissions for Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) to cut roads and install PNG pipelines will be approved within 24 hours after a complete request is submitted. The move is intended to remove procedural obstacles to infrastructure expansion.

The department, which oversees Delhi’s roads, has also waived road restoration charges for three months, through June 30, 2026. This aims to reduce financial and administrative barriers and support faster installation of PNG connections, ensuring that restoration costs do not delay the broader expansion of cleaner energy access.

Officials have emphasized that IGL must treat the work as a priority, complete it promptly, and provide adequate manpower. Areas excavated for pipeline installation must be securely backfilled to protect the public and avoid preventable hazards. The initiative combines the goal of widening access to cleaner energy with expectations of efficient implementation and accountability for public safety and orderly road management.
